title: 6 Best Driveway Sealers in 2026: Asphalt and Concrete Picks
metaDescription: Of 6 driveway sealers, Latex-ite Airport Grade is best for asphalt and Foundation Armor SX5000 for concrete. Picks across both surfaces, compared.
keywords: what is the best driveway sealer
what is the best concrete sealer for driveway
intro:
The best driveway sealer is the one made for your surface: Latex-ite Airport Grade for an asphalt driveway and Foundation Armor SX5000 for a plain concrete one. No single product does both jobs well, so the first decision is what your driveway is made of, and the brand comes second.

This guide splits six picks between the two materials, three for blacktop and three for concrete, and explains why they work in opposite ways. Then it covers how to identify your surface, which sealer type suits your climate, how decorative concrete and pavers change things, and how often each surface needs a fresh coat.
quickAnswer: For asphalt, buy Latex-ite Airport Grade, or Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 for the best finish and Henry to save money. For plain concrete, buy a penetrating silane-siloxane: Foundation Armor SX5000 in most climates, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 where roads are heavily salted. For stamped or exposed-aggregate concrete, Foundation Armor AR350 adds a wet look.

The most expensive driveway sealing mistake is buying the wrong family of product. Asphalt sealer on concrete looks like a tar spill and peels off in sheets. A clear concrete repellent on asphalt has nothing to react with and does nothing. Settle the surface question, then pick within the right family.

For deeper single-surface rankings, see the [best asphalt driveway sealer](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list and the [best concrete driveway sealer](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list. This page is the place to start if you are not sure which one you need.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Driveway Sealers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
Picks are based on each maker's published formula, label coverage and cure requirements, retail availability, and recurring themes in owner reports. No durability scores are invented here; where a claim comes from a label or a data sheet, it is attributed that way.

### Best for Asphalt Driveways: Latex-ite Airport Grade

For blacktop, this is the pail that suits the widest range of driveways. Airport Grade is a water-based asphalt emulsion with mineral filler and polymer, so it has the body to close up the open texture of a driveway that has started to gray, yet it still spreads easily enough for a first-timer with a squeegee. The label asks for the usual window of 50°F and rising with dry weather to follow, and tools rinse clean with water before it cures. Owners commonly report that the color holds through the first year and that the fully cured film resists tire scuffing better than cheap pails. It is never a product for concrete, and it is not a repair for structural cracking or sunken spots, which need patching first. On sound asphalt, it is the most dependable result you can buy off the shelf.

**Pros:** Filled, polymer-modified emulsion covers moderate wear; water cleanup and low odor; stocked widely for batch matching; even black that hides patches.

**Cons:** Heavy filler needs thorough mixing; thirsty on very porous blacktop.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Latex-ite+Airport+Grade+driveway+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Concrete Driveways: Foundation Armor SX5000 WB

SX5000 WB is a water-based silane-siloxane, the category many concrete contractors recommend for exterior driveways. Rather than forming a coat on top, the small silane molecules soak into the pores and react to make them water-repellent, with the siloxane portion helping near the surface. The concrete looks unchanged but sheds water and slows the absorption of dissolved deicing salt, the main driver of winter scaling. With no film, there is nothing to peel, nothing to wear off under tires and no slick surface in rain. Coverage depends on how porous the slab is, and the label recommends testing absorption on a small patch first. Owners commonly report water beading for several years and an easy pump-sprayer application. If you want gloss or a darker color, it is the wrong product; if you want the slab to survive winters, it is the right one.

**Pros:** Penetrates with no visible film or shine; water-based and low odor; cuts water and salt absorption; no slippery surface; pump-sprayer application.

**Cons:** No color change or gloss; will not hide stains or worn finishes.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+SX5000+WB&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Harsh Winters: Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500

Ghostshield positions Siloxa-Tek 8500 as a heavier-duty penetrating sealer for concrete that faces severe winters, and it comes up often in owner discussions about protecting driveways, garage aprons and sidewalks from salt damage. Like SX5000 it is a silane-siloxane blend that sinks in and leaves the surface looking the same, so the choice between them comes down to formulation strength and price rather than appearance. Ghostshield markets it specifically for freeze-thaw and deicer exposure and backs that with detailed application guidance on its data sheet. Owners commonly report strong water beading and like that the same product suits nearby brick and paver walks. It costs more per gallon than many alternatives, which is hard to justify in a mild climate. In the northern states, where scaling can strip a driveway surface within a decade, it is a sensible upgrade.

**Pros:** Formulated for freeze-thaw and salt exposure; invisible, with no film to wear; also suits brick, pavers and masonry; low odor.

**Cons:** Priced above most penetrating sealers; adds no color or gloss.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Asphalt Finish: Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000

Drive-Maxx 1000 is the top tier of Black Jack's driveway line and the pail owners reach for when curb appeal is the priority. It is a water-based emulsion with filler and polymer, and it dries to one of the deepest, most uniform blacks among retail sealers. On a smooth driveway in good condition, that finish is the main reason to pay the premium. On a rough, gray surface the edge narrows, because any filled sealer soaks in on the first coat and needs a second to look even, and a mid-priced filled product handles that for less. Owners praise how easily it spreads and how it looks in the first season; price is the most frequent complaint. Treat the years on the label as a product tier, not a guaranteed interval between coats, and use it on asphalt only.

**Pros:** Very dark, uniform finish; filler and polymer for a tougher film; water-based and easy to apply; widely available.

**Cons:** Top-of-range price; finish advantage shrinks on rough, oxidized asphalt.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Black+Jack+Drive-Maxx+1000&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Wet-Look Finish: Foundation Armor AR350

AR350 is a solvent-based acrylic that forms a thin film and gives concrete a wet, darker, slightly glossy look. That makes it a favorite for decorative concrete such as exposed aggregate, stamped patterns and stained slabs, where the goal is to make color and texture stand out. Acrylic films also resist staining reasonably well while they are intact. The trade-offs are upkeep and traction. Acrylics wear under tires, especially where wheels turn, and most owners recoat every two to three years to keep the look even. A glossy driveway is slippery in rain and snow, so an anti-slip grit in the final coat is strongly recommended on any slope. Owners commonly report that thin coats look better and last longer than thick ones, which can turn milky over trapped moisture. Check your state's VOC rules before ordering.

**Pros:** Rich, wet-look color; popular on exposed aggregate, stamped and colored concrete; solvent formula bonds well; easy to recoat.

**Cons:** Slippery when wet without anti-slip additive; solvent fumes and VOC limits in some states; recoats more often than penetrating sealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+AR350+wet+look+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget Asphalt: Henry Asphalt Driveway Filler & Sealer

Henry's filler-sealer is the budget blacktop product worth recommending. It is a water-based emulsion with modest filler, and it spreads quickly under a squeegee. On a driveway sealed in the last few years that still has a tight surface, one or two coats bring back the color and water resistance at a low cost per square foot, which adds up on long driveways where premium pails get expensive. On badly oxidized asphalt it is less convincing, since the surface absorbs much of the first coat and an even black usually takes a second. Price the full job before assuming the budget pail wins. Owners describe it as a good-value maintenance coat that fades sooner than flagship tiers. It is strictly for asphalt; concrete owners should look at the penetrating sealers above.

**Pros:** Low cost per pail for big driveways; filler handles hairline cracks; water cleanup; good maintenance coat.

**Cons:** Thinner film, so shorter interval before recoating; often needs two coats on porous asphalt.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Henry+asphalt+driveway+filler+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Is Your Driveway Asphalt or Concrete?
sections.body:
Check before you shop, especially on an older or patched driveway. Both materials can look gray, both crack and both get dirty, but the material decides everything about the sealer.

### Signs of asphalt

Asphalt, or blacktop, is stone bound in a black petroleum binder. It flexes slightly and softens on a hot afternoon, when you can often press a key into the surface. It starts black and turns gray as the binder oxidizes, exposing individual stones. It usually has no control joints, and its edges crumble and slope into the lawn.

### Signs of concrete

Concrete is cement, sand and stone cured into a rigid slab. It stays hard at any temperature, starts light gray or white, and has straight cut or tooled control joints every eight to twelve feet. Edges are formed square, and cracks tend to be straighter and sharper. Stamped, colored and exposed-aggregate driveways are all concrete.

### Mixed signals

If you see both, you may have an asphalt overlay on old concrete; treat it as asphalt. Interlocking pavers are a third category: individual concrete or clay units on sand. They take concrete-family sealers, but the joint sand changes the process, which our [best paver sealer](/best-paver-sealer/) guide covers.

sections.heading: Why Do Asphalt and Concrete Need Different Sealers?
sections.body:
Because they fail in different ways, and the sealers that protect them work in opposite directions.

### How asphalt fails

Asphalt ages mostly from the top down through oxidation. Sun and air harden the binder, the surface becomes brittle and porous, fine material washes out and water gets in. Asphalt sealer replaces that lost binder with a fresh sacrificial layer on the surface. It restores the black color and absorbs the UV and wear for two or three years so the pavement does not have to.

### How concrete fails

Concrete does not oxidize the same way. Its main enemy is water, especially water carrying deicing salt. Water soaks into the pores, freezes, expands and pops off thin flakes in a process called scaling. Salt multiplies the freeze-thaw cycles. Concrete sealer protects mostly by keeping water and salt out of the pores.

### What happens when you mix them up

Asphalt sealer on concrete has nothing similar to bond with. It peels, tracks black into the house and makes a light slab look like an oil spill, and removing it takes chemical strippers and pressure washing. A penetrating concrete sealer on asphalt cannot react with the binder and simply evaporates. There is no universal driveway sealer that does both jobs well, whatever a label suggests.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Concrete Sealer for a Driveway?
sections.body:
For a plain broom-finished driveway, a penetrating silane-siloxane. Concrete sealers split into penetrating products that work inside the pores and film-forming products that leave a coating on top.

| Type | Look | Typical reseal | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Silane / siloxane (penetrating) | Invisible | Often 5+ years per label | Plain driveways in salt and freeze climates |
| Lithium or sodium silicate (densifier) | Invisible | Rarely needed | Hardening weak, dusting surfaces |
| Acrylic (film) | Satin to wet-look gloss | About 2 to 3 years | Stamped, colored, exposed aggregate |
| Epoxy / polyurethane | High gloss | Varies | Garage floors, not driveways |

### Penetrating sealers

They do not change the look, do not wear off under tires and are not slippery, and many state transportation departments and concrete industry groups cite them as an effective defense against chloride intrusion.

### Acrylics

Acrylics darken and enrich color and resist staining while intact, but they wear where tires turn and need recoating every few years. Solvent-based acrylics generally bond better than water-based ones but bring stronger fumes and stricter VOC rules.

### Epoxy and polyurethane

Excellent indoors, a poor match outdoors. Most epoxies yellow in UV, and both can trap ground moisture and delaminate. Keep them in the garage, where our [best garage floor epoxy](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) guide applies.

sections.heading: What Asphalt Sealer Do Professionals Spray on Driveways?
sections.body:
Most residential sealcoating crews spray or squeegee a bulk asphalt emulsion or, where it is still legal, a refined coal tar emulsion. They buy concentrate, dilute it, blend in sand and additives, and apply it from a tank rig. Their material is often as good as or better than premium retail pails, and a crew can coat a typical driveway in an hour or two.

### The retail options

Nearly every retail asphalt sealer is a variation on asphalt emulsion: refined asphalt suspended in water with clay, plus filler, sand and polymer. Thin, unfilled emulsions are maintenance coats for smooth driveways sealed recently. Filled emulsions add mineral filler to cover texture and bridge hairline cracks, which is what most aging driveways need. Polymer-modified emulsions add latex or rubber for flexibility and scuff resistance and sit at the top of most brand lines.

### Coal tar and oil-based products

Coal tar resists fuel and oil better, but it carries high levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, stronger odor and skin irritation risk, and it is restricted in Washington, Minnesota and many municipalities. Ask any contractor which base their product uses. Oil-based cutback sealers are a small niche with strong solvent fumes.

### Is sealing worth it at all?

On a structurally sound driveway, usually. Our breakdown of [whether asphalt driveways should be sealed](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/) covers when it pays and when it is wasted money.

sections.heading: How Should Climate Change Your Driveway Sealer Choice?
sections.body:
Where you live should shape the decision almost as much as the surface. A concrete driveway in Arizona and one in Minnesota face different threats, and so does asphalt in Florida sun versus a New England winter.

### Cold climates with road salt

For concrete, a penetrating silane-siloxane is close to essential, and the first two winters matter most because young concrete is most vulnerable. Avoid deicers on new concrete in its first winter if you can, and never use ammonium-based products on any concrete. Our [best ice melt for concrete](/best-ice-melt-for-concrete/) guide sorts products by risk.

For asphalt in cold climates, cracks are the weak point. Water gets in, freezes and widens them each winter, so crack filling before sealing matters more than which pail you buy. Plows and shovels also scrape sealer off, so high-traffic strips wear faster.

### Hot, sunny climates

UV dominates on asphalt, and regular sealing pays off more here than anywhere. For concrete, salt is less of a concern, so the case for sealing rests more on stain resistance and appearance. An acrylic can make sense on decorative concrete, but plain gray concrete in a warm, dry climate can often go without sealer.

### Weather on sealing day

Both surfaces want roughly 50°F and above through the cure, no rain for at least a day, and no scorching pavement. Penetrating concrete sealers can be a bit more forgiving of cool weather than asphalt emulsions, but follow each label. Our guide to the [minimum temperature for sealing a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/) has the details.

sections.heading: How Do You Seal Stamped Concrete, Exposed Aggregate and Pavers?
sections.body:
Decorative driveways are where film-forming sealers earn their place.

### Stamped concrete

Stamped concrete usually has color hardener and release agents on the surface that fade and wash out without a sealer, and the installer almost always applied an acrylic. Recoating with a compatible acrylic is normal maintenance. Switching to a penetrating sealer will not bring back color or sheen, and mixing incompatible acrylics can cause a cloudy, peeling finish.

### Exposed aggregate

A wet-look acrylic such as AR350 brings out the stone colors and helps bind loose fines at the surface. Keep coats thin; thick acrylic puddles in the low spots and turns white if moisture is trapped under it.

### Pavers

Address the joint sand first. Polymeric sand has to cure before sealing, and some sealers are designed to stabilize ordinary joint sand themselves. The [best water-based paver sealer](/best-water-based-paver-sealer-reviews/) guide covers products that suit most paver driveways.

### Test a patch first

On any decorative concrete, try a new sealer on a small, out-of-the-way spot and wait a day before judging. Compatibility problems usually show as whitening, bubbling or lifting within hours.

sections.heading: How Often Should You Reseal Each Driveway Surface?
sections.body:
| Surface and sealer | Typical reseal interval |
| --- | --- |
| Asphalt, water-based emulsion | About 2 to 3 years |
| Concrete, silane-siloxane | 5+ years per many labels |
| Concrete, acrylic film | About 2 to 3 years |
| New concrete before first seal | About 28 days of cure |
| New asphalt before first seal | About 6 to 12 months |

### The water test works on both

Sprinkle water on a dry day. If it beads or runs off, the sealer is still working; if it darkens the surface and soaks in, it is time. On concrete with a penetrating sealer, beading fades first in the tire paths, so test there rather than at the edges.

### Do not over-seal asphalt

Each coat adds thickness, and a heavy buildup cracks and flakes, taking good layers with it. Sealing on a fixed yearly schedule is a common way to cause that.

### Cost per year of protection

A penetrating concrete sealer that lasts five years or more can cost less per year than an acrylic recoated every two to three years, even if the gallon price is higher. On asphalt, money spent on crack filling and prep does more than money spent on a premium pail. For typical DIY and contractor totals, see [how much it costs to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/).

mistakes.title: Using asphalt sealer on concrete
mistakes.body: The costliest mistake on the list. Asphalt sealer does not bond to concrete, peels in sheets within a season, tracks black onto floors and turns a light slab blotchy. Removal takes strippers and pressure washing. If your driveway has straight joints and stays hard on a hot day, it is concrete.

mistakes.title: Sealing new concrete too soon
mistakes.body: Fresh concrete releases moisture for weeks. Sealing early can trap it, leaving a cloudy acrylic film or a poor bond. Wait about 28 days unless the label allows earlier application, and ask your contractor which curing compound they used, since it can affect bonding.

mistakes.title: Rolling acrylic on too thick
mistakes.body: Heavy acrylic coats trap solvent and moisture, which shows up as white haze, bubbles and peeling, and they make the surface slicker. Two thin coats look and bond better than one heavy coat. Add anti-slip grit to the final coat on any sloped driveway.

mistakes.title: Skipping crack repair on asphalt
mistakes.body: Sealer does not fill open cracks. It sinks in, leaves a channel for water and the crack shows again within weeks. Fill anything wider than about 1/8 inch with a dedicated filler and let it cure first. In cold climates, unfilled cracks widen every winter.

mistakes.title: Choosing gloss when you need protection
mistakes.body: A wet look is attractive, but on a plain concrete driveway in a salt-belt climate it is the wrong priority. Acrylics wear under tires and need frequent recoats, while salt-driven scaling is better handled by a penetrating sealer. Settle protection first, then the look.

faqs.q: What is the best driveway sealer?
faqs.a: It depends on the surface. For asphalt, Latex-ite Airport Grade is the best all-round pail, with Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 for the best finish and Henry for budget refreshes. For plain concrete, a penetrating silane-siloxane such as Foundation Armor SX5000 or, in harsh salted winters, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the best choice.

faqs.q: Can one sealer be used on both asphalt and concrete driveways?
faqs.a: No. Asphalt sealers are black emulsions that coat the surface, while concrete sealers are clear products that penetrate the pores or form a clear film. Asphalt sealer peels off concrete and stains it, and concrete repellents have nothing to react with in asphalt. Buy the product made for your surface.

faqs.q: What is the best concrete sealer for a driveway?
faqs.a: A silane-siloxane penetrating sealer, such as Foundation Armor SX5000 or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500. These soak in, leave no visible film, stay non-slippery and reduce water and salt absorption, the main cause of winter surface damage. Choose an acrylic only if you want a darker, glossier look and accept more frequent recoating.

faqs.q: What is the best rated asphalt driveway sealer?
faqs.a: Among widely sold pails, Latex-ite Airport Grade is the strongest all-round choice, based on its filled, polymer-modified formula, availability and owner reports. Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 is the premium pick for smooth blacktop where looks matter. Whatever you buy, expect the coat to last about two to three years.

faqs.q: Is a wet-look sealer bad for a driveway?
faqs.a: Not bad, but it has trade-offs. Wet-look acrylics are slippery when wet, wear under tires and usually need recoating every two to three years. They suit stamped, colored or exposed-aggregate driveways where appearance is the point. On sloped driveways, mix anti-slip grit into the final coat for traction in rain and snow.

faqs.q: Should I seal a brand new driveway?
faqs.a: Yes, but not right away. New concrete typically needs about 28 days of cure before most sealers, though some penetrating products allow sooner. New asphalt needs much longer, usually six months to a year, so its oils can cure out. Sealing either too early leads to poor bonding, so ask your installer for their guidance.

faqs.q: Are coal tar driveway sealers still legal?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live. Washington and Minnesota restrict coal tar sealers statewide, and many cities and counties elsewhere ban their sale or use. Even where legal, they carry stronger odor, skin and eye irritation risk, and runoff concerns tied to PAHs. For a home driveway, an asphalt emulsion is the practical choice.

bottomLine: Start with the surface, not the brand. For plain concrete, buy a penetrating silane-siloxane such as Foundation Armor SX5000, or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 in a harsh, salted climate, and save a solvent acrylic like AR350 for decorative concrete where you accept grit and recoats. For asphalt, Latex-ite Airport Grade is the dependable middle choice, Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 gives the best finish on smooth blacktop, and Henry keeps a sound driveway looking fresh for less. Whatever the surface, clean thoroughly, repair cracks first and seal in a dry, warm window.
